open_obligations: Note that the product-of-wins model assumes step outcomes are independent, so it does not test error propagation directly.
Check that the equal-slope assumption (mG = mH = 1) used for the numerical results is realistic.
Check whether 'oversight success' in Engels et al. corresponds to bounded reward-model error in Leike et al.
in.other_title: Numerical NSO findings: multi-step oversight beats one step as the capability gap grows
in.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether mistakes compound across levels of recursive reward modeling. Engels et al. model nested oversight as a chain whose success is the product of stepwise Guard win probabilities and report that multiple steps can move Guard log odds from -3 to 3, with the optimal number of steps growing with the general capability gap; the model assumes independent steps on fitted Elo lines rather than measuring error propagation.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: how oversight success changes when weak-to-strong oversight is chained over several levels, in an Elo-based model of nested scalable oversight

open_obligations: Check the sample size behind the C2 to C3 drop (last two GAOKAO Math questions only).
Note that the recursion is critique-of-critique, not agents trained to assist in training stronger agents.
Compare with the Human-Human C3 results, which improved, before concluding errors accumulate.
in.other_title: Human-AI: third-order critique accuracy falls below second-order for Qwen2.5-7B math
in.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether errors accumulate or are dampened across recursive levels. Wen et al. report human accuracy of 43.75% (response), 53.12% (critique), 56.25% (C2) and 54.69% (C3) when judging Qwen2.5-7B self-critiques, so the third level falls below the second while staying above the AI's own C2-stage accuracy; this is a critique chain at inference time, not recursive reward model training.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether adding recursive levels of AI-assisted evaluation keeps improving human accuracy, for humans judging Qwen2.5-7B recursive self-critiques on GAOKAO Math

open_obligations: Note that Wu et al.'s levels are subtasks of one policy, not separately trained assistants as in recursive reward modeling.
Check whether the compounding was measured quantitatively or observed qualitatively.
Check whether any self-correcting mechanism of the kind Leike et al. suggest was tried.
in.other_title: Errors compound up the tree; training higher-height tasks is hard
in.rationale: Leike et al. pose whether mistakes of narrower agents lead to larger mistakes higher up. Wu et al. report that policy errors at lower levels compound at each composition task, leading to large top-level errors, and that training on the full tree did not improve performance; their hierarchy is a fixed summarisation tree, not a chain of assistant agents training stronger agents.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether errors at lower levels of a recursive human-feedback hierarchy compound upward, for recursive book summarisation

text: The authors pose as an important open question whether the mistakes of the narrower agent A(k-1) lead to larger mistakes in training A(k), or whether training can be made self-correcting so small mistakes are dampened (e.g. via ensembles or agents trained to find and counteract mistakes). They argue that if error accumulation can be bounded and reward modeling yields aligned agents, the hierarchy could be argued aligned by analogy to induction.
title: Do errors accumulate across levels of recursive reward modeling?
